opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the framing of "SFT versus RL" is sometimes a bit of a false dichotomy. They're really complementary tools, and which one you lean on depends a lot on where you're starting from and what you're trying to achieve.

One thing that surprised a lot of people, including us when we were working on s1, is how far you can get with just supervised fine-tuning on a very small amount of high-quality reasoning data. We took around a thousand carefully curated questions with reasoning traces, fine-tuned a strong base model on them, and got performance on competition math that was competitive with much more expensive pipelines. To me that suggests the base model already has most of the reasoning capability latent in it. SFT on good traces is mostly teaching the model a *format*, a way of thinking out loud, checking its work, backtracking, rather than teaching it fundamentally new skills.

And then there's the test-time scaling side. We found you could control how long the model thinks with something really simple, what we called budget forcing. If the model tries to stop early, you append something like "Wait" and it'll often go back, re-examine its answer, and fix mistakes. So you get this knob for trading compute for accuracy without any RL at all.

That said, RL clearly has a role. SFT is fundamentally imitation. You're bounded by the quality of the traces you distill from, and often those traces come from a model that was itself trained with RL. So in a sense SFT can be a cheap way of inheriting what RL discovered. RL is where you can actually explore and find strategies that weren't in your data, especially when you have verifiable rewards like in math or code. The open questions for me are about how much RL is really adding new capabilities versus sharpening what's already there, and how well it generalizes beyond domains where you can check the answer automatically.

So the way I think about it practically: SFT is incredibly data and compute efficient for getting a model into the reasoning regime, and it's a great baseline everyone should try first. RL is more expensive and finicky, but it's what you need to push the frontier. And honestly I think a lot of the community underestimated how strong the simple baseline was, which is why we wanted to put something minimal and fully open out there.

r001.rationale: The response calls RL’s generalization beyond automatically checkable domains an open question; it does not speculate that RL generalizes better than SFT.

r002.rationale: It says RL can explore strategies with verifiable rewards, but does not explain that RL rewards a better answer regardless of the approach used.

r003.rationale: It describes SFT as imitation from reasoning traces, but does not state that supervision on trace tokens trains the model to follow demonstrated solution approaches.

r004.rationale: The response says RL is more expensive and useful for pushing the frontier, but does not suggest that RL might outperform SFT given more compute.

r005.rationale: The response makes no analogy between SFT and teaching someone how to fish.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that they're really complementary, and a lot of the discourse treats them as if you have to pick one, which I don't think is right.

With supervised fine-tuning, the thing people underestimate is how little data you actually need if the data is good. That was the main finding in our s1 work, right? We took about a thousand examples, carefully selected for difficulty, diversity, and quality, and fine-tuned on those, and you get something that's quite competitive with models trained on orders of magnitude more data. And I think what that tells you is that SFT at that stage is less about teaching the model new knowledge and more about eliciting a format or a behavior. The model already knows how to do a lot of this from pretraining. You're basically showing it, "here's what a long reasoning trace looks like, here's what it looks like to backtrack and check your work," and it picks that up very quickly.

The limitation of SFT is that you're bounded by what's in your data. If your traces come from another model, you're sort of distilling that model, and you're not going to exceed it in any fundamental way. You're also imitating, so if the trace has a wrong step that happens to end in the right answer, you're learning that too.

Reinforcement learning is different because the model gets to explore. You give it a verifiable reward, correctness on math, passing unit tests on code, and it can discover strategies that aren't in any dataset you gave it. That's where you see things like the model spontaneously learning to spend more tokens on harder problems, or developing its own verification habits. And in principle, that's the way to go beyond the teacher. The cost is that it's much more expensive, it's finicky to get right, and it's really dependent on having a reward signal you trust, which is easy for math and code and much harder for most of what people actually want these models to do.

So in practice I think the recipe most people have converged on is: SFT first as a cheap, stable way to get the model into the right region of behavior, and then RL on top to actually push the frontier. And honestly, one thing I'd add is that a lot of the gains people attribute to RL can also come from test-time compute scaling. Something like budget forcing, where you just control how long the model thinks by appending "wait" or stopping it early, gives you a surprising amount of that scaling behavior without any RL at all. So I'd encourage people to be a bit skeptical about where the gains are actually coming from, and run the simple baselines before concluding you need the expensive thing.

r001.rationale: The response says RL can explore strategies absent from the training data and, in principle, go beyond the teacher, presenting an advantage over SFT’s data-bound imitation.

r002.rationale: It describes rewarding correctness on math or passing code tests, but does not say RL rewards a better answer regardless of the approach used.

r003.rationale: It explains that SFT uses examples of reasoning traces, including backtracking and checking, and that the model learns to imitate those demonstrated behaviors.

r004.rationale: The response says RL can push the frontier, but does not suggest it might outperform SFT specifically with more compute.

r005.rationale: The response makes no analogy between SFT and teaching someone how to fish.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as complementary. With supervised fine-tuning, you show the model examples of how you want it to reason, and it learns to imitate those examples. That’s a useful way to get started, but you’re constrained by the quality and diversity of the demonstrations. And you’re training it to reproduce a particular sequence of tokens, even though there may be many valid ways to solve the problem.

With reinforcement learning, you can instead say, “Here’s a problem; try to solve it, and we’ll reward you if your answer is correct.” That gives the model more freedom to explore different approaches. You don’t necessarily need to specify what the reasoning should look like, provided you have a reliable way to evaluate the outcome.

That last part is really the key. For math or coding, you can often check an answer or run tests. For more open-ended tasks, defining a good reward is much harder. So I wouldn’t say RL simply replaces supervised fine-tuning. SFT can give you a useful starting point, and RL can help refine the model’s behavior through feedback. The balance depends on what demonstrations you have and what you can reliably verify.

r001.rationale: It says RL gives the model more freedom to explore approaches, but does not speculate that RL generalizes better than SFT.

r002.rationale: It explains that RL can reward a correct answer without specifying how the model must reason, allowing different approaches.

r003.rationale: It says SFT teaches the model by imitation and trains it to reproduce a particular sequence of tokens from demonstrations.

r004.rationale: The response does not suggest RL might outperform SFT with more compute.

r005.rationale: The response makes no analogy between SFT and teaching someone how to fish.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as complementary. With supervised fine-tuning, you show the model examples of how you want it to solve a problem, and it learns to imitate those examples. That’s a useful way to establish a starting point, but you’re constrained by the quality and diversity of the demonstrations you have.

With reinforcement learning, you let the model generate solutions and give it a reward based on how well it did. For reasoning, that’s especially interesting in domains like math or coding, where you can often check the final answer or run tests. You don’t necessarily have to specify every intermediate step—you give the model room to discover ways of solving the problem.

But I wouldn’t draw too sharp a distinction between imitation and discovery. RL still depends on what the model can explore from its starting point, and getting the reward right is crucial. A model can learn to exploit an imperfect reward without becoming better at the task you actually care about.

So the practical question is: do you have good demonstrations, a reliable way to verify answers, or both? SFT can give you a strong initialization, and RL can then help improve the policy through feedback.

r001.rationale: The response describes RL as allowing exploration, but does not speculate that it generalizes better than SFT.

r002.rationale: It says RL rewards solutions based on how well they did and that final answers can be checked, without requiring every intermediate step.

r003.rationale: It explains that SFT shows examples of desired problem solving and trains the model to imitate those demonstrated approaches.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that RL might outperform SFT given more compute.

r005.rationale: It makes no analogy to teaching someone how to fish.
